chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
title: Ben Webster's sound and playing without a mike
summary: Webster and Hawkins had the biggest tones; a Stuyvesant Casino gig and playing loud without amplification.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: (Unintelligible.)
Yeah, yeah. By the way, did you know Ben Webster at all, either in or out of the band?
Oh, very well.
Because I --
We spent a lot of time together in Europe.
I was very fond of him.
Oh, yeah.
Give me some of your memories of -- impressions of Ben.
You mean, in the band, or --
Just as a person and as a musician. Because a lot of people don't know about him now.
Well, Ben Webster and Coleman Hawkins had the biggest tones in the business. Ben Webster had an even more oozing, soothing tone than Coleman Hawkins. Coleman was harsh.
Yeah.

Ben has a big, beautiful sound. I remember one of my first gigs with Joe Jones, Ben Webster, Charlie Parker, Coleman Hawkins, and I forgot who was on trumpet, probably the guy that used to play with Basie, (unintelligible).
Yeah, right.
And it was at the Stuyvesant Casino. Bob Mule used to his concerts on the weekend.
Oh, sure, yeah.

And there was one mike, and they'd put it -- Bob Mule would make the announcements, put the mike out in front and these guys were standing back, leaning on the wall and playing. They could hear them all over the place, people dancing, talking. And that's where that sound -- you had to have a big sound in those days.
Yeah.
Now, say, (unintelligible) Hamp's band, I had my bass sit up and play loud without a mike. Most people were using an amplifier in those days.
How did you do that, aside from pressure and the like? Was it a matter of tuning or --
No, you'd raise the strings and pull harder.
